Declarations for `neo:fs`. See [host permissions and module access](/runtime/permissions/) before importing.

Bounded filesystem access. Requires `--allow-fs` and a runtime
allowlist that admits `neo:fs`.

During managed module evaluation, `readFile` reads, `writeFile` and
`writeText` write, `stat` and `lstat` read metadata, `readDir` lists a
directory, `mkdir` creates a directory, and `remove` deletes an entry on a
worker. Those eight return Promises. `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`,
`writeTextSync`, `statSync`, `lstatSync`, `readDirSync`, `mkdirSync`,
`removeSync`, and the other operations block the JavaScript thread. Relative
paths resolve
against the runtime's working directory, with no fallback to the host
directory. If that directory is unavailable, the asynchronous forms reject
with `FS_CWD` during a managed turn and synchronous operations throw
`FS_CWD`. Outside a managed turn, the asynchronous forms instead throw
`FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O. Absolute paths and `..` components still
reach everything the host user can reach. This is not a sandbox.

`readFile`, `readFileSync`, `readText`, `writeFile`, `writeFileSync`,
`writeText`, and `writeTextSync` require a regular file.
An open may occur before a non-regular object is rejected. If the type is
identified, the error is `FS_IS_DIRECTORY` or `FS_TYPE`; an open failure
can take precedence. Device-open side effects and latency are not bounded.
Reads are bounded at `MAX_READ_BYTES` and writes at `MAX_WRITE_BYTES`
before an unbounded allocation. A path is
bounded at `MAX_PATH_BYTES`. `FS_LIMIT` also covers quota, storage-full,
and fallible allocation failures; this cannot catch every failure inside
QuickJS or the process allocator.

`stat`, `statSync`, `readFile`, `readFileSync`, `readText`, `writeFile`,
`writeFileSync`, `writeText`, `writeTextSync`, `exists`, `readDir`, and
`readDirSync` follow a symlink at the final path component. `lstat` and
`lstatSync` do not.
`readDir` and `readDirSync` do not follow entries and report a symlink entry
with `isSymlink: true`. `remove` and `removeSync` never follow a symlink at
the target, and recursive deletion does not follow symlinks inside the tree.
An intermediate directory symlink in the path is resolved by the OS, so a
deletion can land inside the link target, outside the apparent tree. They
report parsed roots (including Windows UNC share roots), paths ending in a
separator, and final `.` or `..` components with `FS_PATH`.
A Windows directory symlink named directly as the target is rejected with
`FS_UNSUPPORTED`, even if dangling.

Options accept only the documented own, enumerable data properties.
Accessors, non-enumerable properties, and unknown keys throw `TypeError`;
inherited properties are ignored. A Proxy can run traps during reflective
validation. The runtime-local absolute path and, for binary writes, the
input bytes are snapshotted before those traps run, so a trap that changes
`neo:process.chdir()` or the input buffer cannot redirect that call. A text
write also snapshots its text before resolving the path. A trap may still
reenter the API or run arbitrary script code.

`readDir` and `readDirSync` are not atomic snapshots, and recursive deletion
can be partial if an OS error interrupts traversal. `exists`, `stat`, `statSync`, and
`lstatSync` are
time-of-check/time-of-use snapshots. Do not use them
for access-control or race-free decisions. `writeFile`, `writeFileSync`,
`writeText`, and `writeTextSync` truncate before writing and are not atomic;
a failure can leave a partial file. No write is durable on return, and concurrent writes
have no ordering guarantee. A started asynchronous write may complete its
side effects after a failed turn; cancellation does not roll back. No file
locking is performed. The opened descriptor is verified
before truncation. Unix data opens (including copy) use `O_NONBLOCK` to
avoid waiting for a FIFO peer and `O_NOCTTY` to avoid acquiring a controlling
terminal. Other device-open side effects remain possible, and device and
network filesystem latency is not bounded.

Filesystem failures are `FsError` values with a stable `code` and fixed
messages that never contain the supplied path or an OS error string.
An argument of the wrong type throws `TypeError` from a synchronous
operation and rejects the asynchronous Promise; exceptions from option
proxy traps can propagate or reject likewise.

## FsErrorCode

```ts
/**
 * Stable failure codes reported by `FsError.code`. `FS_PATH` includes
 * invalid or unsupported path syntax and, for `remove`, `removeSync`,
 * `rename`, and `copyFile`, parsed roots, trailing separators, and final `.`
 * or `..` components.
 */
export type FsErrorCode =
  | "FS_PATH"
  | "FS_NOT_FOUND"
  | "FS_NOT_DIRECTORY"
  | "FS_IS_DIRECTORY"
  | "FS_ALREADY_EXISTS"
  | "FS_NOT_EMPTY"
  | "FS_CROSS_DEVICE"
  | "FS_DENIED"
  | "FS_LIMIT"
  | "FS_ENCODING"
  | "FS_DETACHED"
  | "FS_OUT_OF_BOUNDS"
  | "FS_CWD"
  | "FS_TYPE"
  | "FS_UNSUPPORTED"
  | "FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN"
  | "FS_CANCELLED"
  | "FS_IO";
```

## FsError

```ts
/**
 * A filesystem failure. `code` is stable; `message` is fixed text and does
 * not include the supplied path or file contents.
 */
export class FsError extends Error {
  readonly code: FsErrorCode;
}
```

## FileInfo

```ts
/**
 * A metadata snapshot from `stat`, `statSync`, `lstat`, or `lstatSync`.
 *
 * `size` is a decimal string of the exact byte size, never a JavaScript
 * number, so a `u64` value above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` keeps every
 * digit. For a symlink reported by `lstat`, `size` is the host's symlink
 * size, not the target's size. `mtimeMs` is whole milliseconds since the
 * Unix epoch as a decimal string, truncated toward zero (a pre-epoch time
 * less than one millisecond from 1970 is `"0"`), or `null` when the host
 * cannot report the modification time.
 *
 * `stat` and `statSync` follow a final symlink, so their result has
 * `isSymlink: false`. `lstat` and `lstatSync` do not, so a link reports
 * `isSymlink: true` with `isFile` and
 * `isDirectory` both `false`. A non-regular path that is neither a file, a
 * directory, nor a symlink has all three flags `false`.
 */
export interface FileInfo {
  readonly isFile: boolean;
  readonly isDirectory: boolean;
  readonly isSymlink: boolean;
  readonly size: string;
  readonly mtimeMs: string | null;
}
```

```ts

export interface DirEntry {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly isFile: boolean;
  readonly isDirectory: boolean;
  readonly isSymlink: boolean;
}
```

```ts
  /**
   * `true` (the default) creates or truncates the file. `false` uses

   * by the open call, not a prior `exists` check.

  overwrite?: boolean;
}
```

## readText

```ts
/**
 * Read a regular file as UTF-8 text.
 *
 * The file must be a regular file. Files larger than `MAX_READ_BYTES`
 * throw `FS_LIMIT` before the file is read. Invalid UTF-8 throws
 * `FS_ENCODING`. A missing path throws `FS_NOT_FOUND`; a directory or
 * other non-regular object may be opened before rejection, and the OS
 * open error can take precedence. This preserves the original `readText`
 * signature; the new bound and `FsError` shape are the documented migration.
 */
export function readText(path: string): string;
```

## writeText

```ts
/**
 * Write UTF-8 text on a worker, creating the file or truncating an existing
 * one, using the runtime directory captured at the call.
 *
 * **Breaking change:** this function was synchronous. Use
 * `await writeText(path, data)` during managed module evaluation, or
 * `writeTextSync(path, data)` in synchronous code. Outside a managed turn
 * this throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O. A non-string `data`
 * rejects the Promise with `TypeError`.
 *
 * Text exceeding `MAX_WRITE_BYTES` in UTF-16 code units is rejected with
 * `FS_LIMIT` before export. Otherwise any unpaired surrogate rejects with
 * `FS_ENCODING`, even if the text also exceeds the UTF-8 byte limit.
 * Well-formed text exceeding `MAX_WRITE_BYTES` in UTF-8 bytes then rejects
 * with `FS_LIMIT`. The text snapshot is taken before the path is resolved.
 *
 * Parent directories are not created. A final symlink is followed, so a
 * dangling link can create its target. Writing is not atomic. An I/O
 * failure can leave the destination empty or partially written; there is
 * no temporary file, rename, rollback, or cleanup. There is no durability
 * guarantee. Concurrent writes have no ordering guarantee.
 *
 * A text write shares the four-operation outstanding bound and two-worker
 * pool with the other asynchronous filesystem operations, and charges its
 * UTF-8 byte length plus the encoded byte length of its resolved path
 * against the same turn budget. Excess work rejects with `FS_LIMIT`. The
 * owned UTF-8 snapshot can briefly coexist with the caller's string and the
 * worker-owned buffer.
 *
 * If the turn fails, teardown requests cancellation, but an OS call that
 * has already started cannot be interrupted. A started text write may
 * therefore still create, truncate, or fully write the file after the turn
 * has failed or its Promise has been abandoned; those side effects are not
 * rolled back. There is no caller cancellation API. Turn teardown cancels
 * cooperatively and may wait for an OS call to return.
 */
export function writeText(path: string, data: string): Promise<void>;
```

## writeTextSync

```ts
/**
 * Write UTF-8 text, blocking the JavaScript thread.
 *
 * The same text validation, error precedence, path, symlink, truncation,
 * side-effect, and concurrency rules as `writeText` apply, except that
 * failures throw instead of rejecting and the call returns `undefined`.
 */
export function writeTextSync(path: string, data: string): void;
```

## readFile

```ts
/**
 * Read a regular file on a worker, using the runtime directory captured
 * at the call. Only available during managed module evaluation; otherwise
 * throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O. In a managed turn, invalid
 * arguments and I/O errors reject the Promise. A module turn accepts up
 * to four outstanding filesystem operations (including undelivered
 * results) and runs up to two on workers. Metadata and directory reads
 * share this bound but charge their path plus a small metadata or listing
 * result bound; a directory creation or deletion charges its path. Each
 * outstanding read charges `MAX_READ_BYTES` plus the encoded byte length of
 * its resolved path
 * against a shared turn budget of
 * `4 * (max(MAX_READ_BYTES, MAX_WRITE_BYTES) + MAX_PATH_BYTES)`.
 * Excess work rejects with `FS_LIMIT`. This budget does not cover buffers
 * JavaScript retains after delivery. There is no caller cancellation API.
 * Turn teardown cancels cooperatively and may wait for an OS call to return.
 * Use `readFileSync` to block.
 */
export function readFile(path: string): Promise<Uint8Array>;
```

```ts
/**
 * Read a regular file as bytes, blocking the JavaScript thread.

 * Returns a `Uint8Array` view over a new buffer. The same regular-file and
 * `MAX_READ_BYTES` rules as `readText` apply. The result is a copy, not a
 * live view of the file.
 */
export function readFileSync(path: string): Uint8Array;
```

## copyFile

```ts
/**
 * Synchronously stream bytes from a regular file into a new regular file.
 * Both relative paths use the same runtime cwd. Roots, trailing separators,
 * and final `.` or `..` components throw `FS_PATH`. On Windows, copy rejects
 * UNC, device, drive-relative and drive-less rooted paths, reserved device names, alternate
 * data streams, and ambiguous trailing dots or spaces in components.
 *
 * Unlike the reference copy API, this never overwrites or copies metadata.
 * The source may be a symlink to a regular file; exclusive creation
 * refuses an existing destination (`FS_ALREADY_EXISTS` when reported by
 * the OS), including aliases and dangling links. Parents are not created.
 * Copy can span filesystems. The limit is `MAX_READ_BYTES`; an oversize
 * source detected at open throws `FS_LIMIT` before creating anything.
 *
 * This is not atomic or durable. A failure after creation (including
 * growth past the limit) can leave a partial file, which is not removed.
 * Concurrent renames or writes can change which paths or bytes are seen.
 * No-clobber depends on the filesystem honoring exclusive creation.
 */
export function copyFile(source: string, destination: string): void;
```

## writeFile

```ts
/**
 * Write bytes to a regular file on a worker, using the runtime directory
 * captured at the call. Only available during managed module evaluation;
 * otherwise throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O.
 *
 * The input must be a `Uint8Array`; a `DataView`, another typed array, or a
 * `Proxy` throws `TypeError`. A detached buffer throws `FS_DETACHED`, an
 * out-of-bounds view throws `FS_OUT_OF_BOUNDS`, and a `SharedArrayBuffer`
 * view throws `FS_UNSUPPORTED`. The view's live bytes and the resolved path
 * are copied before reflecting on options. In a managed turn, invalid
 * arguments and I/O errors reject the Promise. By default the file is
 * created or truncated before writing. Parent directories are not created,
 * and the write is not atomic.
 *
 * If the turn fails, teardown requests cancellation, but an OS call that
 * has already started cannot be interrupted. A started write may therefore
 * still create, truncate, or fully write the file after the turn has failed
 * or its Promise has been abandoned; those side effects are not rolled
 * back. An I/O failure can leave the destination empty or partially
 * written; there is no temporary file, rename, rollback, or cleanup. There
 * is no durability guarantee: a fulfilled Promise does not mean the data
 * reached stable storage. Concurrent writes have no ordering guarantee;
 * final contents depend on their interleaving at the OS and filesystem
 * level.
 *
 * A module turn accepts up to four outstanding filesystem operations
 * (including undelivered results) and runs up to two on workers. Each write charges its
 * copied byte length plus the encoded byte length of its resolved path
 * against a shared turn budget of
 * `4 * (max(MAX_READ_BYTES, MAX_WRITE_BYTES) + MAX_PATH_BYTES)`; reads
 * charge `MAX_READ_BYTES` instead of their actual length. Excess work
 * rejects with `FS_LIMIT`. The asynchronous form copies the JavaScript
 * snapshot into worker-owned memory, so a large write can briefly hold the
 * caller's input, the snapshot, and the worker copy. This budget does not
 * cover buffers JavaScript retains after delivery. There is
 * no caller cancellation API. Turn teardown cancels cooperatively and may
 * wait for an OS call to return. Use `writeFileSync` to block.
 */
export function writeFile(
  path: string,
  data: Uint8Array,
  options?: WriteFileOptions,
): Promise<void>;
```

## writeFileSync

```ts
/**
 * Write bytes to a regular file, blocking the JavaScript thread.
 *
 * The input, view, and option validation and the error precedence match
 * `writeFile`, except that failures throw instead of rejecting. The view's
 * live bytes and the resolved path are copied before reflecting on options.
 * By default the file is created or truncated before writing. Parent
 * directories are not created, and the write is not atomic.
 *
 * An I/O failure can leave the destination empty or partially written;
 * there is no temporary file, rename, rollback, or cleanup. There is no
 * durability guarantee: returning does not mean the data reached stable
 * storage. Concurrent writes have no ordering guarantee; final contents
 * depend on their interleaving at the OS and filesystem level.
 */
export function writeFileSync(
  path: string,
  data: Uint8Array,
  options?: WriteFileOptions,
): void;
```

## stat

```ts
/**
 * Read metadata for a path on a worker, following a final symlink. Only
 * available during managed module evaluation; otherwise this throws
 * `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O. In a managed turn, invalid arguments
 * and filesystem errors reject the Promise. Metadata work shares the
 * four-operation outstanding bound and two-worker pool with `readFile` and
 * `writeFile`, and charges its path plus a small result bound against the
 * same turn budget. Excess work rejects with `FS_LIMIT`. There is no caller
 * cancellation API; turn teardown cancels cooperatively and may wait for an
 * OS call. See `FileInfo` for the result representation.
 */
export function stat(path: string): Promise<FileInfo>;
```

## exists

```ts
/**
 * Test whether a path exists, following a final symlink.
 *
 * Returns `false` for a missing path, a dangling symlink, or a path below a
 * non-directory. Other failures, notably permission denial, throw. This is
 * a snapshot and must not be used for race-free access-control decisions.
 */
export function exists(path: string): boolean;
```

## readDir

```ts
/**
 * List a directory on a worker, non-recursively.
 *
 * **Breaking change:** this function was synchronous. Use
 * `await readDir(path)` during managed module evaluation, or
 * `readDirSync(path)` in synchronous code. Outside a managed turn this
 * throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O.
 *
 * In a managed turn, invalid arguments and filesystem errors reject the
 * Promise. Directory work shares the four-operation outstanding bound and
 * two-worker pool with `readFile`, `writeFile`, `stat`, and `lstat`, and
 * charges its path plus a bounded listing result against the same turn
 * budget. Excess work rejects with `FS_LIMIT`. Entries are sorted by name in
 * UTF-8 byte order and bounded by `MAX_LIST_ENTRIES`, `MAX_LIST_NAME_BYTES`,
 * and `MAX_LIST_TOTAL_BYTES`; exceeding a bound rejects with `FS_LIMIT`.
 * Entry types are not followed. A final symlink to a directory is followed.
 *
 * Turn teardown checks cancellation between entries, before the explicit
 * no-follow metadata fallback, and before sorting. A cancelled listing rejects with
 * `FS_CANCELLED` and never resolves with a partial array. An initial
 * `read_dir` call and an individual metadata call are not interruptible once
 * started; teardown joins the worker and may wait for them to return. There
 * is no caller cancellation API.
 */
export function readDir(path: string): Promise<DirEntry[]>;
```

```ts
 * The same path, sorting, symlink, bound, and error rules as `readDir`
 * apply, except that failures throw instead of rejecting. A name that is

 */
```

## mkdir

```ts
/**
 * Create a directory on a worker.
 *
 * **Breaking change:** this function was synchronous. Use
 * `await mkdir(path, options)` during managed module evaluation, or
 * `mkdirSync(path, options)` in synchronous code. Outside a managed turn
 * this throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O.
 *
 * In a managed turn, invalid arguments and filesystem errors reject the
 * Promise. Without `recursive`, an existing path reports `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS`
 * and a missing parent reports `FS_NOT_FOUND`. With `recursive: true`,
 * missing parents are created and an existing directory is accepted. No
 * `mode` option is provided.
 *
 * Creation shares the four-operation outstanding bound and two-worker pool
 * with the other asynchronous filesystem operations, and charges its
 * resolved path against the same turn budget. Teardown cannot interrupt a
 * creation that has started: it may still create some or all directories
 * after a failed turn, and cancellation never removes a created directory.
 * An OS or network failure can leave a partial tree with no rollback.
 *
 * On Unix, a non-recursive creation refuses a final symlink, including a
 * dangling one, with `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS` and never follows it. Recursive
 * creation accepts a final symlink to an existing directory but reports
 * `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS` for a dangling final symlink. Both forms follow
 * intermediate symlinks, so creation can land outside the apparent parent
 * tree. A non-recursive path below a dangling intermediate symlink reports
 * `FS_NOT_FOUND`; the recursive form reports `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS`. An
 * intermediate component that resolves to a non-directory reports
 * `FS_NOT_DIRECTORY`. A final path occupied by an existing regular file
 * reports `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS` in both modes.
 *
 * These rules are path-based and are not containment. A component can be
 * replaced between path resolution and the OS call, redirecting creation
 * elsewhere. Windows reparse-point, junction, and symbolic-link semantics are
 * platform-specific; this build does not assert them.
 */
export function mkdir(path: string, options?: MkdirOptions): Promise<void>;
```

## mkdirSync

```ts
/**
 * Create a directory, blocking the JavaScript thread.
 *
 * The same creation, option, error, final and intermediate symlink, and
 * no-containment rules as `mkdir` apply, except that failures throw instead
 * of rejecting. An OS or network failure can leave a partial tree with no
 * rollback.
 */
export function mkdirSync(path: string, options?: MkdirOptions): void;
```

## remove

```ts
/**
 * Remove a file, symlink, or directory on a worker.
 *
 * **Breaking change:** this function was synchronous. Use
 * `await remove(path, options)` during managed module evaluation, or
 * `removeSync(path, options)` in synchronous code. Outside a managed turn
 * this throws `FS_ASYNC_OUTSIDE_TURN` before I/O.
 *
 * In a managed turn, invalid arguments and filesystem errors reject the
 * Promise. Without `recursive`, a non-empty directory reports
 * `FS_NOT_EMPTY`. With `recursive: true`, the whole tree is removed without
 * following symlinks. A final symlink is removed as a link, except that a
 * Windows directory symlink is reported as `FS_UNSUPPORTED`. Parsed roots
 * (including Windows UNC share roots), trailing separators, and final `.` or
 * `..` components report `FS_PATH` before I/O. There is no undo, no trash,
 * and no count limit.
 *
 * Deletion shares the four-operation outstanding bound and two-worker pool
 * with the other asynchronous filesystem operations, and charges its
 * resolved path against the same turn budget. Teardown cannot interrupt a
 * deletion that has started: it may still remove some or all entries after a
 * failed turn, cancellation restores nothing, and an OS or network failure
 * can stop a recursive deletion part-way with no rollback.
 *
 * A final symlink is removed as a link, never followed, and recursive
 * deletion uses the OS-backed tree removal, which does not follow links
 * inside the tree. An intermediate directory symlink in the path is
 * resolved by the OS, so deletion can land inside the link target, outside
 * the apparent parent tree.
 *
 * It is pathname based and is not containment: an intermediate component
 * can be replaced between validation and the OS call
 * (time-of-check/time-of-use), and the runtime neither canonicalizes the
 * target nor reverses a deletion. Windows reparse-point, junction, and
 * symbolic-link semantics are platform-specific; this build does not assert
 * them.
 */
export function remove(path: string, options?: RemoveOptions): Promise<void>;
```

```ts
/**

 * that failures throw instead of rejecting.
 */

```

## rename

```ts
/**
 * Synchronously rename a file, directory, or symlink entry. Both relative
 * paths use the same runtime working directory. Final symlinks are not
 * followed, and replacement follows the host OS rules.
 * A rejected replacement of a non-empty directory can throw
 * `FS_ALREADY_EXISTS` or `FS_NOT_EMPTY`, depending on the OS error.
 *
 * Both paths must name specific entries: parsed roots, trailing separators,
 * final `.` or `..`, and Windows drive-relative paths throw `FS_PATH`.
 * Neither path is canonicalized on disk; joining a relative path to a
 * Windows verbatim working directory can normalize intermediate components
 * lexically.
 * The runtime never pre-deletes the destination, creates parents, or falls
 * back to copy/delete. An OS cross-device error throws `FS_CROSS_DEVICE`.
 * Paths can change between resolution and use; there is no sandbox, rollback,
 * or guarantee of the outcome after an OS or network filesystem failure.
 */
export function rename(source: string, destination: string): void;
```
